task: I'm 42 with a resting heart rate of 58 bpm. Using the Karvonen method, what are my five training heart rate zones? Give me the bpm range for each zone.

deeper: I'm 42 with a resting heart rate of 58 bpm. Using the Karvonen method, what are my five training heart rate zones? Give me the bpm range for each zone.

answers.plain:
**Assumptions:** Max HR = 220 − 42 = **178 bpm**, so Heart Rate Reserve (HRR) = 178 − 58 = **120 bpm**.

Formula: Target HR = (HRR × %intensity) + resting HR

| Zone | Intensity | Range (bpm) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 – Very light (recovery) | 50–60% | 118–130 |
| 2 – Light (aerobic/base) | 60–70% | 130–142 |
| 3 – Moderate (tempo) | 70–80% | 142–154 |
| 4 – Hard (threshold) | 80–90% | 154–166 |
| 5 – Maximum (VO₂ max) | 90–100% | 166–178 |

The zones share boundaries (130, 142, 154, 166). Treat each boundary as the top of the lower zone or the bottom of the upper one, as you prefer.

**Caveat:** 220 − age is only an estimate, and real max HR can differ by 10 bpm or more. If you've measured your max HR in a hard effort or a test, swap it in for 178 and the zones will be more accurate.
answers.nudge:
# Karvonen heart rate zones (age 42, resting HR 58 bpm)

**Inputs**
- Estimated max HR: 220 − 42 = **178 bpm**. The Tanaka formula (208 − 0.7 × age) gives 178.6, so both agree.
- Heart rate reserve (HRR): 178 − 58 = **120 bpm**
- Formula: target HR = (HRR × intensity %) + resting HR

| Zone | Intensity (% HRR) | Range (bpm) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 – Recovery | 50–60% | **118–130** | Warm-up, cool-down, active recovery |
| 2 – Aerobic base | 60–70% | **130–142** | Fat oxidation, mitochondrial and aerobic base, long easy sessions |
| 3 – Tempo | 70–80% | **142–154** | Aerobic power, steady "comfortably hard" efforts |
| 4 – Threshold | 80–90% | **154–166** | Lactate threshold, raising sustainable pace |
| 5 – VO₂max | 90–100% | **166–178** | Short intervals, maximal aerobic capacity |

**How to refine these**
1. **Measure your max HR.** The formulas have a standard deviation of about ±10 bpm. After a warm-up, do a field test: 3 minutes hard, 3 minutes easy, then another 3 minutes all-out, and note the peak. If your true max is, say, 185, every zone above rises. Don't do this if you have cardiac risk factors or haven't been training. Get medical clearance first.
2. **Use a true resting HR.** Take it on waking, lying down, averaged over 5–7 days. If it drifts (poor sleep, illness, overtraining), your zones shift with it. A resting HR that is elevated by 5 bpm or more for several days is a signal to back off.
3. **Anchor to threshold if you can.** A 30-minute time trial (the average HR over the last 20 minutes approximates lactate threshold HR) is more individual than any percentage. Lab lactate or ventilatory testing is better still.
4. **Use a 3-zone check.** Most of your volume (roughly 75–80%) should be in Zones 1–2, with hard work (Zone 4–5) limited to 1–2 sessions a week. Zone 3 is the "gray zone" that is easy to overuse.
5. **Allow for drift.** Heat, dehydration, caffeine, hills and fatigue raise HR by 5–10 bpm at the same effort. Use perceived effort (the talk test in Zone 2) alongside the numbers.
6. **Know the limits.** Beta blockers and some other medications blunt HR. In that case, use RPE instead.
answers.skill:
**Setup**
- Max HR (220 − age): 220 − 42 = 178 bpm
- Heart rate reserve (HRR): 178 − 58 = 120 bpm
- Target HR = (HRR × intensity %) + 58

**Zones**

| Zone | Intensity | Range (bpm) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 – Very light (recovery) | 50–60% | 118–130 |
| 2 – Light (aerobic base) | 60–70% | 130–142 |
| 3 – Moderate (tempo) | 70–80% | 142–154 |
| 4 – Hard (threshold) | 80–90% | 154–166 |
| 5 – Maximum (VO₂ max) | 90–100% | 166–178 |

**Calculations**
- 50%: 60 + 58 = 118
- 60%: 72 + 58 = 130
- 70%: 84 + 58 = 142
- 80%: 96 + 58 = 154
- 90%: 108 + 58 = 166
- 100%: 120 + 58 = 178

The 220 − age formula is only an estimate, and actual max HR can differ by 10 bpm or more. If you've measured your max HR in a hard effort or test, use that number instead. The zones will shift accordingly. Adjacent zones share boundary values, so at 130 bpm, for example, treat yourself as being at the Zone 1/2 border.
